title: Baby Nudges: How Social Influences Shape Fertility Choices | Institute for Family Studies
gist: IFS/Wheatley survey of nearly 10,000 people in a dozen-plus countries finds fertility intentions track peer and parental support, admired celebrities, personal joy in children, risk tolerance and active faith, but not moral obligation norms or household labor division; East Asia's low social support stands out.

insights.claim: Fertility varies enormously among groups sharing the same economic environment: from 2010 to 2026 Ultra-Orthodox Jews in the New York metro averaged 7.5 births per woman versus 1.58 for college-educated native-born non-Hispanic white women, and Ohio Amish average about 6 while Ohio is below 2.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Cross-group gaps under identical costs show that material policy alone cannot explain fertility; culture is a separate lever.
insights.locator: From 2010 to 2026, Ultra-Orthodox Jews

insights.claim: The report is based on a survey of nearly 10,000 people in over a dozen countries (US to Israel to Korea), plus a database of family behavior among historic and current elites with Wikidata or Wikipedia pages, to open the 'black box' of fertility culture.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Defines the evidence base; findings are associations from survey data, not experiments.
insights.locator: We used a survey of nearly 10,000 people

insights.claim: In every country studied except Israel, actual fertility is below the family size respondents say would make them happiest, even in Egypt where birth rates of about 2.3-2.4 undershoot stated desires of 2.4-2.6.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: An unmet-desire fertility gap implies pronatal policy aimed at helping people reach their own goals has a wide addressable base.
insights.locator: in every country we studied besides Israel

insights.claim: Perceived friend support for childbearing predicts fertility: believing friends would celebrate a new baby is associated with a 10% higher desired number of children and a 20% higher likelihood of intending another child.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Social-support infrastructure is a measurable correlate of fertility intentions, especially for first births.
insights.locator: Friends and family matter to fertility intentions.

insights.claim: The US, UK and Israel report the highest friend alloparental support, while Chinese-speaking Asia, Japan and Korea report very little; only 4% of Japanese and 6% of Korean respondents expect meals from friends after a baby versus over 20% of Americans.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: East Asian parenting isolation is a structural reason for ultra-low fertility there; policies must address social support, not just cash.
insights.locator: over 20% of our American respondents believe their friends will bring them meals

insights.claim: The gap between the lowest and highest countries on friend and family support predicts roughly a whole extra child in intended family size and about half a child in children ever born.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Gives a magnitude for cross-country social-support effects.
insights.locator: Index of expected friend supportiveness

insights.claim: Supportive friends mainly raise intentions to have a first child and have almost no association with trying for a third to fifth child, so peer effects concentrate where recent fertility declines have been largest.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Interventions on peer culture should target childless young adults.
insights.locator: As can be seen below, having supportive friends

insights.claim: Social reaction to births turns more negative as families grow: people with three or more kids report more negative reactions, and mainland China has the highest rate of worry over family-size discrimination.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Social penalties on larger families may cap progression to third and later births.
insights.locator: We find that people with 3 or more kids report more negative reactions

insights.claim: Admiring a public figure with a bigger family than one's own is associated with a 14% higher likelihood of intending another child, and changes in elite fertility or visibility have historically predicted changes in population fertility.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Media and influencer family norms are a plausible fertility lever; the survey measure was crude (one admired figure per respondent).
insights.locator: Admiring a public figure with a family bigger

insights.claim: Japan's fertility fell sharply after satellite TV arrived in 1984 and amplified largely childless idol culture, and South Korea began falling toward lowest-low fertility after idol culture appeared in the early 1990s, with K-pop stars penalized for revealing relationships.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Elite childlessness norms in entertainment may amplify low fertility; the authors acknowledge economic confounders such as the Plaza Accord and 1997 Asian financial crisis.
insights.locator: In 1984, satellite TV came to Japan.

insights.claim: In Britain, elite fertility fell during the 1700s while general fertility rose, and the 1877 Knowlton Trial exposed elite family limitation to the public and triggered wider adoption of contraception; the authors generalize that elites are early adopters of low-fertility norms followed by non-elite 'catch-down' declines.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: A historical template: when elite behavior becomes visible, mass fertility can shift rapidly.
insights.locator: But, in 1877, the “Knowlton Trial,”

insights.claim: Average admired-celebrity family size is about one child in Japan and 1.7 in Korea but over 2.5 in Israel and Egypt.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Cross-country gap in celebrity family size tracks national fertility differences.
insights.locator: In Japan, the average admired celebrity

insights.claim: General pronatal norms (belief people have a moral obligation to have children) do not predict intending another child or children born, whereas personal attitudes such as seeing children as the greatest joy do.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Duty-based pronatal messaging is ineffective; joy-based framing is the evidence-backed approach.
insights.quote: “pronatal” general norms are not pronatal in effect or consequence
insights.locator: Baby Fever: Personal Attitudes vs. Social Obligations

insights.claim: Mainland China has the highest share (about 16%) saying most people have an obligation to have children, yet its fertility is below 1 child per woman.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Illustrates the disconnect between stated norms and fertility outcomes.
insights.locator: the country where respondents are likeliest to say

insights.claim: Believing children are a serious burden is associated with a 19% lower chance of intending a child and a 24% lower desired family size among the childless; childless people are far likelier than parents to call parenting a burden, suggesting they overestimate its difficulty.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Information and exposure to real parenting may raise first-birth intentions.
insights.locator: Childless young people's erroneous beliefs

insights.claim: Rivalrous values such as pet parenting satisfaction and desire to protect leisure are negatively associated with all fertility indicators, whereas travel is not.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Alternative life-meaning sources compete with family formation.
insights.locator: Satisfaction from “pet parenting”

insights.claim: Parental encouragement to have children is associated with an 11% higher desired number of children and 30% higher likelihood of intending another; encouragement to marry predicts a 14% higher intention among partnered childless respondents.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Family-level nudges matter; framed around joy and offers of help rather than guilt.
insights.locator: Parents encouraging their children to become parents

insights.claim: Willingness to take risks, social trust, clear view of the future, and belief that life is getting better all predict higher fertility; low-fertility Japan and Korea rate their risk tolerance lowest while Americans and Egyptians rate highest.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Anxiety and safety-ism are candidate drivers of fertility decline; risk-hedging policy could help.
insights.locator: Respondents’ self-rated willingness to take risks

insights.claim: The authors suspect social media is the primary culprit for rising risk intolerance, and respondents spending at least two hours daily on social media have about 5% lower desired family sizes.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Supports regulatory and design scrutiny of algorithmic social media as a fertility factor.
insights.locator: We suspect there is a simple primary culprit

insights.claim: Top-third religiosity is associated with 9% more children, 15% higher desire for more children and 12% higher intention to have another; going from the least religious countries (Japan, China) to the most (Egypt) adds about one child to intended family size.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Religious participation remains one of the strongest fertility correlates.
insights.locator: Being in the top third of respondents in religiosity

insights.claim: Within countries, how often religious leaders speak about family has no detectable association with fertility; religion's effect appears to run through friend and congregant support rather than leader exhortation.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Pronatal religious messaging from leaders is overrated; community support networks are what matter.
insights.locator: Religious leaders’ frequency of explicit exhortations

insights.claim: Division of household labor and perceived fairness of chores do not significantly predict fertility desires or intentions, and countries where women feel more unfairly burdened actually have higher birth rates.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Undercuts the thesis that equalizing chores will raise fertility; East Asia's problem is total labor load, not division.
insights.locator: Contrary to popular narratives, unequal division

insights.claim: The authors recommend fertility policy focus on making family life joyful rather than appeals to duty, including airport family lounges, date-night child care, prenatal matching of expectant parents, and remote work and on-site daycare framed as family benefits.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Signals the policy menu of the pronatalist movement, which favors amenities and risk-hedging over pure cash.
insights.locator: Focus fertility policy on making family life pleasant

insights.claim: The authors suggest hedging downside risk for young families through measures such as more generous unemployment insurance, voucher-based school choice, and an American Birthday Account giving newborns an immediate nest egg, and they raise regulating algorithmic social media.
insights.speaker: Lyman Stone
insights.so_what: Pronatalist policy proposals that could appear in legislation; algorithm regulation is an open question.
insights.locator: Take the fear of downside risk
